saks-global-bankruptcy-approved.headline: Saks Global bankruptcy plan wins court approval
saks-global-bankruptcy-approved.body_md:
A federal bankruptcy judge in Houston cleared Saks Global Enterprises LLC on Friday to proceed with what amounts to the largest luxury retail restructuring in recent memory, approving a reorganization plan that slashes the company's debt by nearly 75 percent and transfers ownership to senior lenders.

Judge Alfredo Perez of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas confirmed the plan at a June 5 hearing, saying the company had done an "extraordinary" job stabilizing operations after a difficult start to the case. Saks Global — parent of Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus and Bergdorf Goodman — filed for Chapter 11 on January 13, just 13 months after completing its $2.7 billion acquisition of Neiman Marcus Group, a deal that left it carrying $3.4 billion in debt and unable to pay key vendors.

The post-emergence balance sheet looks materially different. Debt falls to approximately $1.2 billion — a $750 million term loan plus a $347 million ABL facility — supported by nearly $700 million in liquidity. The exit financing tranche of $500 million was committed by Pentwater Capital Management and Bracebridge Capital, which had also provided $1 billion in debtor-in-possession financing during the case and are stepping in as new equity owners. Nearly 720 brands that suspended shipments during the restructuring have resumed, and $1.6 billion in retail receipts have been released back into the supply chain.

## A smaller company, with long-range targets

The surviving store footprint consists of 49 luxury locations: 33 Neiman Marcus stores, 15 Saks Fifth Avenue outlets and the Bergdorf Goodman flagship. Off-price divisions were wound down entirely; Horchow and 14 standalone Fifth Avenue Club locations closed during the case.

Junior creditors received a $20 million litigation trust — added after court objections — but face minimal recovery on the bulk of their claims. Original equity was extinguished. Management's stated targets run to $9 billion in gross merchandise value and double-digit adjusted EBITDA by fiscal 2030, with 2026 EBITDA of $85 million tracking ahead of plan and 2027 projected at roughly four times that level as cost savings compound. Profitability on a net basis is not projected until fiscal 2029.

CEO Geoffroy van Raemdonck, who took the role at the time of the January filing, framed the outcome as repositioning rather than rescue: a company with "three incredible banners" and a capital structure capable of investing in growth rather than servicing legacy acquisition debt.

For fixed-income holders and retail-sector equity desks, the confirmation order removes the near-term governance overhang. What it does not yet supply is granular visibility into store-level unit economics, the pace at which dropped vendor assortments return to full depth, or how the slimmed-down Saks fares against specialty luxury formats that gained ground during the five-month case. The company expects formal emergence around June 22 — that date, and the first set of post-bankruptcy operating metrics that follow, will be the more telling signal.

trump-warsh-rates-october.headline: Trump says he wants lower rates, may leave October decision to Warsh
trump-warsh-rates-october.body_md:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he would like to see lower interest rates but will leave the rate decision to Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh when the Federal Open Market Committee meets in October — a notably hands-off formulation from a president who has spent much of his political career haranguing the central bank.

"Housing's all about interest rates," Trump said at a community college event. "They can pass all the bills they want, it's about interest rates. You get the interest rates down, everybody's going to be very, very happy." Asked separately on Fox Business whether he still expects rates to fall, he answered: "When Kevin gets in, I do... interest rates should be much lower."

The pivot to deference — 'I'll leave it to Warsh' — is the unusual part. Trump has long preferred the direct approach, publicly pressuring Jerome Powell for cuts and, after years of frustration, replacing him. Installing Warsh was itself meant to signal a dovish shift. Saying he will now stand aside and let the new chair handle October reads less as restraint and more as expectation management: Trump is telling the housing market, the bond market, and his own political base that relief is calendared, if not guaranteed.

## The Math Is Not Cooperating

The problem is the economic data, which has turned sharply in the wrong direction for rate-cut advocates. The May payrolls report released Friday showed 172,000 jobs added — more than double the consensus forecast of roughly 85,000 — while March and April were revised up by a combined 93,000. The three-month average now sits at 188,000. Unemployment held at 4.3%. Consumer prices are running at 3.8% year-on-year, the hottest reading since May 2023 and nearly double the Fed's 2% target.

Markets processed this quickly. CME FedWatch data now puts the odds of at least one rate *hike* in 2026 above 57%, with October specifically pricing better than 60% for tightening. The 2-year Treasury yield — the most sensitive instrument to near-term rate expectations — jumped to 4.15%, while 20- and 30-year bonds crept above 5%.

Warsh, who was sworn in at the White House on May 22 as the first Fed chair to take the oath there since Alan Greenspan in 1987, has been deliberate about keeping distance from the White House's preferred outcome. He testified during his confirmation hearing that Trump had not asked him to "predetermine, fix or decide on any interest rate decision." He holds one of 12 FOMC votes. Jerome Powell, whom Trump sought for years to remove, remains on the board as a sitting governor through 2028 and retains the ability to influence committee deliberations.

The October 27–28 FOMC meeting carries an additional layer of complexity: it falls less than a week before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections, at which all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up. The Fed's informal tradition of avoiding rate moves that could be read as politically timed will make any October cut — or hike — a harder lift to narrate as purely technical.

For now, the specific catalyst to watch is Warsh's first meeting as chair on June 16–17, when the FOMC will release updated economic projections alongside its rate decision. Markets are pricing no action there. What the 'dot plot' signals about the second half of the year will set the frame for whether October is even in play.

nasdaq-jobs-four-horsemen-macro.headline: Jobs surprise hands Nasdaq its worst day since the tariff shock as four market risks converge
nasdaq-jobs-four-horsemen-macro.body_md:
For most of the spring, the story on Wall Street was simple: AI chips were infallible, the Federal Reserve was finished tightening, and a nine-week winning streak for the S&P 500 suggested investors had decided to move on from last year's tariff turbulence. Friday's May jobs report demolished all three assumptions before the opening bell.

> **In brief:** Strong May payrolls doubled Wall Street's consensus estimate, sent rate-hike bets surging, and triggered the Nasdaq 100's worst single session since the April 2025 Liberation Day shock — dragging semiconductors, AI proxies, and bitcoin down with it.

## The number that flipped the script

U.S. employers added 172,000 jobs in May, roughly double the ~85,000 consensus forecast. Prior months were revised upward by a combined 93,000. The unemployment rate held at 4.3%. On its own the report might have been read as a sign of resilience; layered on top of an April CPI print of 3.8% year-over-year — the hottest reading since May 2023 — it was enough to shift the entire rates narrative.

The bond market responded immediately. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.54%; the 30-year crossed 5%. Money markets, which had spent weeks pricing in a prolonged Fed pause or even cuts, swung sharply in the other direction: by Friday afternoon, futures implied a 96% probability of at least one rate hike before year-end. That is a material repricing from where consensus sat just a week earlier.

Hotter-than-expected hiring alongside stubbornly elevated inflation removes the Fed's principal reason to stand still. The question is no longer whether it cuts — it is whether it hikes.

## The Nasdaq's worst session since Liberation Day

The rate shock detonated squarely in the corner of the market most exposed to it. The Nasdaq 100 fell 4.7%, its worst single-day loss since the April 2025 tariff shock that briefly erased trillions from global equities. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.18%, closing at 25,709. The S&P 500 shed 2.6%, snapping a nine-week winning streak — the longest such run since 2023. The Dow held up comparatively, losing 1.4%.

The damage concentrated in semiconductors. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell roughly 9% on Friday and is now down more than 10% over two sessions. Marvell Technology lost 16%; Micron declined 13%; AMD, Arm, Intel, and Qualcomm each shed more than 10%.

Broadcom (AVGO) illustrated the difficulty of beating numbers when the macro frame has shifted. The company reported earnings that exceeded expectations on Thursday and reiterated AI revenue guidance of "in excess of $100 billion" — a figure that would have been received as bullish news a month ago. Instead, shares collapsed 12.6% Thursday and gave up another 7% on Friday. When a company posts strong results and still falls double digits across two sessions, the problem is not the fundamentals; it is the discount rate applied to every future dollar of profit.

![Broadcom's Hyderabad campus — AVGO shed nearly a fifth of its value over two sessions despite beating earnings](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/14/Broadcom_Inc.jpg)

The broader growth-stock selloff reflects a straightforward valuation mechanic: higher long-term interest rates compress the present value of distant earnings. Technology and AI names carry more of their value in years five through twenty than, say, a regulated utility or an energy major. A 50-basis-point move in the 10-year yield is a modest number in fixed-income terms but a meaningful one in equity discounting arithmetic.

## Crypto's worst week since FTX

Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since Donald Trump's election victory in late 2024 — a level the market had treated as psychological bedrock. The intraday low reached $59,100 before a partial recovery. The weekly decline stands at roughly 17-19%, the worst seven-day performance since the FTX collapse in November 2022.

Coinglass data showed $1.75 billion in liquidations in the 24-hour period, with 351,233 traders wiped out across crypto markets. Ether performed even worse, losing more than 17% on the week. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows exceeding $3.2 billion.

Strategy Inc. (formerly MicroStrategy), whose stock serves as a leveraged proxy for bitcoin, dropped roughly 25% on the week. Separately, CEO Michael Saylor sold 32 bitcoin for approximately $2.5 million — his first disclosed sale since December 2022 — a move that attracted attention given its timing.

Analysts at Presto Research attributed the crypto selloff partly to competition: as AI equities and gold both reassert themselves as inflation hedges and growth bets respectively, the narrative justification for crypto premium valuations weakens. The rate-hike repricing compounds the problem; risk assets that performed well under an easy-money thesis are the most exposed when the thesis reverses.

## Four risks converging on a concentrated market

The week's events did not arrive in isolation. A separate analysis of S&P 500 structural vulnerabilities identified four compounding pressures that had been building before Friday's data point provided a spark.

First, inflation: the April CPI reading and a commodity backdrop with structural upward pressure mean the Fed's job is not finished, even if the market spent weeks pretending otherwise. Second, technology speculation: the VanEck Semiconductor ETF entered the week up approximately 60% year-to-date and trading 50% above its 200-day moving average — extended by any historical standard. Third, credit stress: private-credit funds have begun restricting redemptions, a signal that liquidity is tightening at the margin in corners of the financial system that do not show up in public spreads. Fourth, concentration: the top ten stocks in the S&P 500 now represent roughly 40% of the index's total market capitalisation — one of the highest readings in modern market history, meaning index-level volatility amplifies any rotation out of mega-cap names.

![The Marriner S. Eccles Building, Federal Reserve headquarters in Washington — rate-hike bets surged to 96% probability after Friday's jobs data](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Marriner_S._Eccles_Federal_Reserve_Board_Building.jpg)

The parallel being drawn in some corners of the market is to late 1999, when investors dismissed Warren Buffett's preference for quality companies during the dot-com bubble. Berkshire Hathaway, Procter & Gamble, and PepsiCo are currently trading at multi-year relative lows versus the broader index — a defensive rotation waiting, in that framing, to happen.

The key question is whether Friday was a corrective shock that clears excess or the beginning of a more durable derating of growth assets. The answer depends almost entirely on what comes next in the data. June's CPI print, due in the second week of July, will be the first real test of whether April's 3.8% reading was a seasonal blip or a trend re-acceleration. The Federal Open Market Committee meets July 29-30 — the meeting at which a rate hike would first be live. Between now and then, the market will have four weeks of data, a string of Fed speaker appearances, and whatever surprises the geopolitical calendar delivers. The earnings season and AI investment cycle are not over. But the era of pricing in cuts and ignoring inflation is.

us-mexico-auto-chinese-content.headline: Washington presses Mexico to cut Chinese content from North American vehicles
us-mexico-auto-chinese-content.body_md:
Washington is negotiating to rewrite the rules governing what goes into a North American vehicle — and the central target is Chinese-made components flowing through Mexican factories into U.S. showrooms. The first formal bilateral round of the USMCA joint review concluded in Mexico City on May 29; a second round is scheduled for Washington on June 16-17, and a third for Mexico City the week of July 20. The July 1, 2026 treaty deadline — mandated under Article 34.7 of the agreement — will pass without a concluded deal. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said plainly that he will not "rubber-stamp an extension" and that the administration "probably will not resolve all the issues by July 1."

What happens after July 1 depends on whether all three parties — the U.S., Mexico, and Canada — agree to extend the pact, which would add 16 years to its life. If any party declines, mandatory annual reviews begin, running for a decade before expiration. Canada, largely sidelined from the bilateral U.S.-Mexico track, has its own complications: Prime Minister Mark Carney's recent agreement admitting 49,000 Chinese-built electric vehicles at reduced tariffs drew a sharp reaction in Washington. For now, Mexico is the priority partner, and the agenda is explicit.

## Rules that remake the supply chain

The core U.S. demand is a higher U.S.-specific content threshold for vehicles built in Mexico. The current USMCA requires that 75% of a vehicle's value originate within North America, with at least 40% of passenger car content (45% for pickup trucks) coming from higher-wage facilities — primarily in the U.S. or Canada — covering core parts like engines, transmissions, and body panels. Washington is now pushing for a 50% minimum for U.S.-specific content alone, a condition the Trump administration also sought, unsuccessfully, during the original USMCA negotiations.

On steel, negotiators want a "melted and poured in North America" requirement for any steel receiving preferential tariff treatment — a provision aimed at blocking Chinese steel processed in Mexico from qualifying for USMCA benefits. Steel industry executive Barry Zekelman, who has been briefed on the talks, described the approach as a systematic effort to "close all of the loopholes that still exist."

Greer has framed the objective broadly: "Over the course of these negotiations, we are going to be talking about rules of origin in a way that enhances U.S. content in these goods." The U.S. also wants to expand the definition of "core parts" to include major electronics modules — a category where Asian supply chains dominate — and is seeking Mexico to align its tariffs on non-USMCA steel with U.S. rates.

The talks are proceeding without congressional trade promotion authority, which means any substantive changes to the USMCA's legal text would require a congressional vote. The practical consequence: officials on both sides expect outcomes to take the form of side letters or protocols rather than formal treaty amendments.

## The China problem inside North American cars

![A Geely auto assembly line in Ningbo, China — one of dozens of Chinese manufacturers expanding into global supply chains](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/55/Geely_assembly_line_in_Beilun%2C_Ningbo.JPG)

The animating concern behind the content push is straightforward: more than 30 Chinese auto-parts manufacturers now operate in Mexico, and the number is rising. In 2024, Chinese-origin vehicle body parts and accessories imported into Mexico were valued at $899 million, representing 13.9% of Mexico's total imports in that category. Major Chinese EV makers — BYD, Geely, Chery, and Great Wall Motor — have been evaluating or bidding for manufacturing capacity in Mexico, seeing the country as a potential springboard into the U.S. market.

U.S. officials and trade analysts describe Mexico as a potential "backdoor" through which Chinese components, or vehicles assembled with Chinese supply chains, can enter North America duty-free under USMCA rules that were written before Chinese automotive investment in Mexico became significant. Research from Brookings and the Rice Baker Institute has found evidence that Chinese products have been circumventing U.S. tariffs via third-country manufacturing — a practice the revised content rules are designed to close off.

Mexico has begun moving in Washington's direction. On January 1, 2026, Mexico imposed a 50% tariff on auto companies without operating plants in Mexico and levied new duties on approximately 1,400 Chinese-origin products. USMCA utilization among Mexican exporters jumped from 44.8% in January 2025 to 88.7% by November 2025, signaling that manufacturers are scrambling to qualify under existing rules — and will need to re-qualify if the thresholds tighten.

## What the market is reading into this

![An auto assembly line — the kind of North American manufacturing the U.S. content push is designed to expand](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f1/Hyundai_car_assembly_line.jpg)

Equity markets registered the trade pressure on publication of the FT's reporting Thursday. Ford fell 3.94%, Stellantis 3.28%, and General Motors 1.27%; the iShares MSCI Mexico ETF dropped 2.77%, and the iShares China Large-Cap ETF shed 1.80%. The moves reflect two distinct risks: for the automakers, compliance costs and supply-chain restructuring if U.S.-content thresholds are raised; for Mexico-linked plays, the possibility that tighter origin rules raise effective costs for manufacturers assembled south of the border.

The deeper implication is what this negotiation signals about other sectors. Auto supply chains are the highest-profile test case for Washington's broader reshoring agenda, but the logic — raise North American content thresholds, restrict Chinese-affiliated inputs, align partner tariffs — is transferable to electronics, batteries, critical minerals, and steel. CSIS analysts have described the review as a potential foundation for "Fortress North America," a systematic reduction of the continent's supply-chain dependence on China. The U.S. International Trade Commission launched its own full review of USMCA automotive rules in February 2026, with a final report due July 2027 — ensuring the pressure on manufacturers persists well beyond any near-term deal.

The next concrete data point is the Washington round on June 16-17. Neither side expects a breakthrough — but movement on the steel and electronics provisions would signal how far Mexico is willing to go before the July 1 clock runs out.

caterpillar-backlog-guidance-2026.headline: Caterpillar hits record backlog, raises 2026 outlook
caterpillar-backlog-guidance-2026.body_md:
Caterpillar entered 2026 with its order book fuller than it has ever been. The Deerfield, Illinois manufacturer reported first-quarter revenues of $17.4 billion — up 22% from the same period a year earlier — and said its backlog had swelled to a record $63 billion, a $28 billion jump that represents 79% growth year over year. Management responded by raising its full-year 2026 sales forecast to low-double-digit growth, lifting guidance that was already pointed upward when the year began.

"Backlog grew to a record level of $63 billion, an increase of $28 billion or 79% compared to the first quarter last year," CEO Joe Creed said on the earnings call late April. "We have a disciplined strategy of scaling capacity in direct alignment with our growing backlog."

Adjusted earnings per share came in at $5.54, up 30% year over year, while gross margin reached 33.1% — the highest reading in eight quarters. Operating income of $3.09 billion was up 17%.

## Power leads; construction follows

The clearest story inside the results is power generation. Caterpillar's Power & Energy segment posted $7 billion in revenue, up 22%, with power generation sales specifically surging 48% — driven almost entirely by data center buildout. The company's large reciprocating engine backlog has grown more than 3.5 times since it first announced an expansion plan in January 2024, and management is now targeting nearly 3x the engine capacity it held in 2024, adding roughly 15 gigawatts of annual output when investments between 2027 and 2029 come online.

Construction Industries, the company's largest segment by revenue at $7.2 billion, grew 38%, with dealer inventory builds contributing alongside seven-percent growth in direct sales to end users — the fifth consecutive quarter of user-level demand expansion. Segment profit jumped 50%, even as tariff-related headwinds bit 550 basis points out of the margin.

Resource Industries — mining and quarrying equipment — grew just 4% to $3.8 billion, with margins contracting 700 basis points to 10%. The culprit was tariffs, compounded by product-mix timing. The offsetting signal: order intake in the segment hit its highest level since 2012, driven by copper and gold mining investment.

On tariffs broadly, Caterpillar fared better than it had projected. First-quarter tariff costs landed at roughly $600 million against an $800 million estimate, and the full-year estimate was revised down to $2.2–$2.4 billion from a prior $2.6 billion figure. Incoming CFO Kyle Epley — taking the seat from Andrew Bonfield, who stepped down after this call — noted that excluding tariff drag, the company expects to finish the year in the top half of its adjusted operating profit margin target range.

Caterpillar also returned $5.7 billion to shareholders in the quarter, including a $4.5 billion accelerated share repurchase, a signal that management views the current capital position as comfortable even as it commits to multi-year capacity expansion.

The next set of numbers to watch will be the second-quarter report, where management has guided for roughly $700 million in tariff costs — slightly above the first-quarter pace. Analysts will also be tracking whether the Power & Energy backlog continues to expand or begins converting to revenue faster, a shift that would confirm capacity investments are keeping pace with demand.

tapestry-coach-gen-z-entry.headline: Tapestry's post-earnings dip offers an entry into Coach's Gen Z franchise
tapestry-coach-gen-z-entry.body_md:
Tapestry reported the kind of earnings quarter that usually rewards shareholders: $1.92 billion in revenue, up 23% year-over-year, a 62% surge in earnings per share to $1.66, and full-year guidance lifted to roughly $7.95 billion. The company's flagship Coach brand added 2 million new customers in a single quarter, 800,000 of them from Gen Z. The stock fell roughly 10% anyway.

That gap between operational momentum and market reaction is the signal worth examining.

## The Goldilocks brand

Coach has spent several years engineering what its chief executive Todd Kahn calls "expressive luxury" — the Goldilocks position between LVMH-tier aspiration and mass accessibility. Most of its handbags are priced between $300 and $700, reachable for a young professional buying a first luxury piece but still carrying the cachet of a heritage New York label founded in 1941. The strategy is working with a demographic that other affordable-luxury names have struggled to capture. North American Coach revenues rose 27% in the fiscal third quarter; Greater China surged 58%; Europe added 27%. Core leather goods volumes grew over 20%, and footwear — driven mainly by sneakers — expanded roughly 20% as well. Coach brand revenue crossed $1.7 billion for the quarter, up 31%, representing approximately two-thirds of Tapestry's group sales.

Kahn's assessment of the addressable opportunity is expansive to the point of near-evangelical: "We can literally add millions of new customers every quarter for the next 10 years, and we'll just scratch the surface." CEO Joanne Crevoiserat frames the target simply: Coach becoming "a $10 billion brand over time, with best-in-class margins."

Against that backdrop, the selloff requires an explanation that goes beyond the brand.

The stock entered results day having already doubled from its 52-week low of $75.48, touching an all-time high of $161.97 in late February. A trailing P/E north of 55 meant perfection was priced in, and perfection is a high bar. What the quarter delivered was close — but not uncomplicated. Kate Spade, the group's second brand, posted a 10% revenue decline to around $220 million and absorbed 180 basis points of tariff-related margin pressure. The company framed the Kate Spade contraction as a deliberate promotional pullback and repositioning effort. The market, reading two-thirds growth and one-third drag, settled on a "sell the news" verdict after an enormous run. A February disclosure that Crevoiserat sold $7.6 million in stock added a note of caution that lingered.

The post-earnings price around $140 is where analysts see value. Fifteen of 21 covering the stock rate it a buy, with a mean 12-month price target of $163.63 — approximately 17% above current levels. Evercore ISI trimmed its target to $175 on May 8 while maintaining an Outperform rating, implying 25% upside from the post-selloff print. GlobalData managing director Neil Saunders notes that Tapestry has effectively become a Coach pure-play: fixing Kate Spade matters, but it no longer makes or breaks the investment thesis.

The case against buying the dip is essentially a valuation argument: even post-correction, Tapestry is not cheap relative to traditional luxury retail multiples, and any further Kate Spade deterioration would test margin guidance. The case for it is that 31% brand revenue growth and accelerating Gen Z penetration at a $300–$700 price point represents a structural, multi-year story — one that a single quarter's profit-taking doesn't invalidate.

The next hard data point is Tapestry's fiscal fourth-quarter report, due in August. Kate Spade's trajectory in that print — whether the promotional discipline produces a revenue stabilization or a continued slide — will determine whether the current entry point looks obvious in hindsight or merely early.

congress-berkshire-abel-exit.headline: Two lawmakers exit Berkshire as Abel settles into the CEO seat
congress-berkshire-abel-exit.body_md:
Congressional stock-trade filings drop every week — a dozen sales, a handful of buys, a disclosure lag of 30 to 45 days — and most carry roughly the same informational weight as a recycled bin. Two recent sales of Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares fall squarely in that category, whatever headline link is drawn to Warren Buffett's retirement.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey, reported two sales of BRK/B on 4 May, each in the $1,000-to-$15,000 range — the lowest mandatory disclosure band. The trades are barely a rounding error for Gottheimer, one of Congress's most prolific stock traders: more than 3,500 transactions on the books, representing north of $340 million in total value. He bought Berkshire shares twice in 2024 and sold them twice in 2025. Nothing in the rhythm suggests a verdict on the new management.

Rep. Christian Menefee, freshman Democrat of Texas, sold three tranches of BRK/B on 10 February totalling between $31,000 and $115,000. These were his first disclosures since entering Congress in January — meaning the stock was already in hand before he cast a single vote. He sold; he hasn't bought back. But the absence of a follow-on purchase tells us very little when the opening position arrived as pre-existing inventory, not a conviction trade.

Two lawmakers, no shared timing, no coordination, different transaction sizes. The pattern is congressional routine, not a post-Buffett referendum.

## Abel's Q1 was the real story

![Greg Abel, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Greg_Abel.jpg/250px-Greg_Abel.jpg)

While the disclosure filings generated heat, the more substantive Berkshire news lay in the company's 13F filing for Q1 2026 — the first full quarter with Greg Abel in the chief executive's chair. Abel was decisive. Berkshire exited 16 positions outright: the entirety of its Visa and Mastercard stakes, its holdings in UnitedHealth Group, Amazon, Domino's Pizza, and Charter Communications, among others. The conglomerate spent roughly $16 billion acquiring stocks while selling around $24 billion — a net-seller posture that trimmed the equity portfolio from 42 holdings to 29.

The buys carried a different disposition from Buffett's late-career caution. Berkshire more than doubled its Alphabet stake, lifting its Class A position to 54.2 million shares valued at roughly $23 billion — vaulting it to the seventh-largest holding. A new position in Delta Air Lines arrived at 39.8 million shares, about $2.8 billion. The company nearly tripled its stake in The New York Times Company and added to its positions in homebuilder Lennar.

All this played out against a backdrop of mild underperformance: BRK shares are down about 1.3% in 2026, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF has gained 8.3% over the same stretch. Some of that gap may reflect genuine investor uncertainty about the post-Buffett era; some is likely mean reversion after decades of outperformance. Neither congressional seller will help settle that question.

The next meaningful read on Abel's evolving approach comes with the Q2 13F filing, due in mid-August. That will show whether Q1's concentrated reshuffling — tech-heavy, airline-curious, media-friendly — was a one-off clearing exercise or the opening chapter of a substantially different investment philosophy.

white-house-ai-natsec-policy.headline: White House bars national security AI from censorship and surveillance as Trump plans industry summit
white-house-ai-natsec-policy.body_md:
On Thursday, the White House signed a presidential memorandum that formally prohibits the national security enterprise from using artificial intelligence to censor speech, embed ideological bias, or conduct surveillance outside constitutional limits. The document — National Security Presidential Memorandum 11, or NSPM-11 — is the most direct statement yet from the Trump administration on what government-linked AI systems are and are not permitted to do.

The timing is not coincidental. Three months ago, the Pentagon blacklisted one of the country's largest AI companies for drawing exactly those lines.

## What NSPM-11 Actually Says

The memorandum lays out four pillars for how the national security enterprise — a term that covers at least thirteen departments and agencies, from the CIA and FBI to the Departments of State, Energy, and Homeland Security — is meant to handle AI. The administration calls them Adoption, Adaptation, Assurance, and Accountability.

The accountability language is the sharpest. Section 2(d) states that "American AI technologies shall neither be developed nor used by the national security enterprise to censor free speech, embed ideological bias, or conduct unauthorized or unlawful surveillance activities." Civil liberties and constitutional protections, the document says, are "non-negotiable."

Enforcement is a different question. The primary mechanism is a chain of command: commanders, directors, and agency heads are made personally accountable for compliance at every level. There is no independent watchdog or inspector-general mechanism named in the text. Section 3(b) does give agencies the authority to terminate contracts with vendors that have "repeatedly demonstrated a pattern of conduct inconsistent with" the stated policies, but that language is permissive — it allows such terminations rather than mandating them.

The document replaces the Biden administration's NSM-25, which Trump officials describe as having burdened AI adoption with "ideological mandates" and fostered "dangerous single-vendor dependencies." Key implementation deadlines fall at 90 days — when the Department of War must update its directive on autonomous weapons — and 120 days, when procurement reviews and a new computing roadmap are due.

## The Anthropic Backdrop

There is an awkward precedent sitting behind all this declared principle. On February 27, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply chain risk to national security. President Trump followed the same day, directing every federal agency to cease using Anthropic's technology. The company was penalized, according to court filings and reporting, because it refused to let the Pentagon use its Claude models without restrictions — specifically, Anthropic had drawn two redlines: no use in autonomous lethal weapons systems, and no use in mass surveillance of American citizens.

In other words, Anthropic was blacklisted for trying to enforce something very close to what NSPM-11 now instructs the government itself to observe.

A California federal judge later blocked the Pentagon's designation as unconstitutional. The Ninth Circuit declined to reinstate the blacklist pending appeal, leaving a split outcome: Anthropic can work with civilian agencies but remains locked out of Defense Department contracts while litigation continues. A spokesperson for Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment on the new memorandum.

![The White House, Washington D.C.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e1/White_House_Washington.JPG)

The Anthropic case illustrates the gap between stated policy and actual enforcement. The administration's AI procurement decisions have operated largely through executive and military authority — quick, difficult to challenge — while the new memorandum relies on diffuse accountability structures rather than any external check. Absent a dedicated oversight body, whether NSPM-11's censorship and surveillance restrictions will constrain procurement choices in practice remains an open question.

## A Summit, and Something Bigger

Also on Thursday, Trump told reporters that he planned to host the leading AI companies at the White House "maybe next week," saying "all of them" would have representatives present. He named no specific companies or agenda items.

The meeting arrives against a broader policy push. On June 2, Trump signed a separate executive order inviting major AI developers to voluntarily submit frontier models to the government for up to 30 days of security testing before public release — a measure the administration describes as a national-security screening tool. Critics note the word "voluntarily" does most of the work; there is no compulsion mechanism.

A more significant idea is now in circulation. According to reporting by The Washington Post and Notus, Trump and his advisers are discussing the possibility of the federal government acquiring equity stakes in major AI companies, framed as a way to give ordinary Americans a share of the industry's profits. OpenAI's Sam Altman has reportedly discussed voluntarily ceding shares to the government. Anthropic, by contrast, is described as not engaging in those conversations — hardly surprising given the ongoing litigation.

The equity-stake concept has no legislative basis yet and faces obvious governance complexities. But its emergence alongside NSPM-11 suggests the administration is thinking about AI in national security terms that go beyond procurement standards — as a strategic asset to be co-owned, not merely regulated.

The next concrete marker is the 90-day deadline for the Department of War's weapons-autonomy update, which falls in September. The courts will continue to shape the Anthropic dispute in parallel. How the AI industry summit goes — and whether the government equity idea moves from White House corridor talk into formal proposal — will do more than any declared principle to reveal what this administration actually intends.

state-dept-ebola-38m.headline: State Department commits US$38m more to Ebola response
state-dept-ebola-38m.body_md:
The U.S. State Department announced on June 5 that it would commit nearly $38 million in additional funding to its Ebola response, bringing the department's total direct contribution to the current outbreak to more than $200 million. The disbursement is the latest increment in what has become a rapidly scaling U.S. engagement since the World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in mid-May.

At the centre of that emergency is a Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak that first surfaced in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri Province before spreading to North Kivu, South Kivu, and — critically — across the border into Uganda, including cases in Kampala. As of early June the outbreak had produced 471 confirmed cases and 84 deaths, a case fatality rate of roughly 18 percent.

## What makes this outbreak harder to contain

The Bundibugyo strain is a complicating factor. Unlike the Zaire ebolavirus behind the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic, there is no licensed vaccine or approved therapeutic for Bundibugyo. The WHO has explicitly recommended against using existing Zaire-targeted vaccines, citing insufficient evidence of cross-protection. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations is fast-tracking three candidates, but none is near deployment.

That scientific gap, combined with the outbreak's foothold in an active conflict zone in eastern DRC, has put severe pressure on containment. Health authorities estimate that only about 20 percent of contacts are currently being traced — a figure that makes controlling transmission geometrically harder with each passing week when chains of infection multiply unseen.

The new $38 million will flow to implementing organizations supporting contact tracing, border and point-of-entry screening, dedicated isolation and treatment facilities, and community education countering misinformation about how the virus spreads. State Department partners have already established six specialized treatment facilities and are supporting 43 clinics across the affected zones. An earlier commitment funded up to 50 new response clinics through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. In Uganda, more than 100 health screeners and data personnel have received training; thousands of frontline workers — including healthcare staff, teachers, and religious leaders — have received community-response instruction.

The United States describes itself as the largest single financial contributor to the current response. The State Department's $200 million envelope sits alongside $350 million committed through OCHA for broader humanitarian needs in the DRC, South Sudan, and Uganda, part of a $1.8 billion U.S. package to UN humanitarian operations announced in May.

For health-equity investors, the appropriation carries limited direct signal. Government aid disbursements do not move clinical timelines, regulatory decisions, or commercial revenue for drug developers. The more consequential catalysts to watch are CEPI's accelerated vaccine candidates and any WHO efficacy data on filovirus platforms — developments that could meaningfully reshape commercial prospects for companies with assets in that space.

floor.headline: The Exhaustion Trap
floor.body_md:
The bot's control-rule strategy hunts yesterday's strongest movers and buys at open, betting on continuation. Today that bet failed across all nine positions. BRSHF, a foreign OTC name that spiked 100% the day before on a thin-market print, crashed £1,466.92 into the scheduled exit. MAC.L peaked before open—up 82.5% overnight but intraday price completely static, zero continuation found.

The bot bought yesterday's winners without filtering for conviction—no volume check, no follow-through test, no thesis gate. When the overnight moves exhausted before open, scheduled exits became forced losses. Nine trades, nine losers.

Tomorrow: does the rule need a conviction filter before entry, or should the bot stop chasing overnight spikes that exhaust before market open?

floor.body_md: TPL (+9.69%) offered no clear catalyst—audit whether coverage gaps buried the signal entirely. MRNA (+7.49%) spiked on June 1 ASCO melanoma-vaccine data, an event-calendar signal that front-ran technical triggers by multiple sessions. SNDK (+6.71%) and FDXF (+6.26%), newly-public via spinoffs, fell to price-per-share and history-length floors. Post-signal strategies cannot retroactively position on pre-announcement data or pre-open news flow. Fixing these systematic misses requires calendar-event coverage layers, spinoff-inclusion logic, or pre-market data ingestion pipelines.
